1.e4 g6 2.d4 Bg7.strategy: The point of the set-up: Black lets White build a broad centre and aims the bishop at it from a distance along the long diagonal, planning to undermine it later with a pawn break. The knights stay flexible and castling comes soon. The price is space, since White holds the centre and Black's counterplay starts slowly.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 d6.strategy: Controls e5 and c5 and keeps several set-ups open, with the bishop on the long diagonal or the knight on f6. The pawn also supports a later ...e5 or ...c5, but until then White has a free hand in the centre.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6.name: Modern Defence: Norwegian Defence
1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6.background: Also called the North Sea Variation. Magnus Carlsen calls the continuation 3.e5 Nh5 the “Norwegian Rat”, and he played it, with 4.Be2 d6, against Michael Adams at the 2010 Khanty-Mansiysk Olympiad.
1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 at once, but 3.e5 gains space with tempo, and the knight has no comfortable square. With no pawn on d6 to challenge e5, Black stays cramped for a gambit that does not repay it.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 c6.strategy: Supports ...d5 and still allows ...d6, so Black can challenge the centre at once or choose a quieter fianchetto set-up. Sound, but less flexible than developing the bishop first, because the c-pawn is committed before the bishop is out.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once and can lead into a Sicilian with an early ...g6. White can take space or open the position, and if Black regains a captured pawn with the queen, it comes out early and costs time.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 d5.strategy: Strikes at e4 at once, but with no pawn behind it, 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 gains time against the queen. After 3.e5 White has an advance structure in which a bishop on g7 bites on e5, and Black must find counterplay quickly. Sound enough, but it concedes time or space.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 against e4 alongside ...Bg7, but it is the wrong order: White develops and supports e4 while Black has made two pawn moves and no piece move. The idea is sound later, but here it gives White time and a lasting edge.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5, but with ...g6 already played the dark squares f6 and h6 are weak and the c8-bishop is shut in behind e6. White develops freely and keeps the broader centre.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nc6.strategy: Pressures d4, but 3.d5 drives the knight away at once and Black loses time. The natural 3...Ne5? even loses a piece to 4.f4, because c4, d3, f3, g4 and c6 are all covered.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, heading for c7 or b4, and does nothing against d4 and e4. 3.Bxa6 bxa6 doubles Black's a-pawns at the cost of the bishop pair, and otherwise White builds freely.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Bh6.strategy: Invites 3.Bxh6 Nxh6, which trades off the dark-squared bishop that the ...g6 set-up exists for and leaves a knight on the rim. White keeps the pawn centre and Black has no counter to it.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where both forward squares are covered: f5 by the e4-pawn and g4 by the queen. The centre goes unchallenged, and White simply develops.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 and ...Bb7 and takes b5 from White's bishop, a useful waiting move. It contests neither d4 nor e4, though, so White is free to take more space; sound, but second-rate next to developing the bishop.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rook's pawn while d4 and e4 stand unopposed, and the pawn can no longer cover b5 from a6. White simply develops.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 f6.strategy: Takes e5 from White but blocks the f6 square and the long diagonal of the future g7-bishop, while doing nothing to challenge d4 and e4. White simply builds up.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 h6.strategy: Wastes a tempo on a rim pawn that contests neither d4 nor e4. The pawn is safe, since 3.Bxh6 Bxh6 wins a piece, but White simply builds up.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 h5.strategy: Weakens g5 and g6 for good and develops nothing. White uses the tempo to develop or take space, and a piece on g5 can no longer be challenged by ...h6.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 b5.strategy: Hangs a pawn for nothing: 3.Bxb5 Bb7 is met by 4.Nc3, which defends e4, and White keeps the extra pawn with a lead in development.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 e5.strategy: Gives away a pawn: after 3.dxe5 nothing recaptures it, and ...Bg7 followed by ...d6 is met by Nf3, so White keeps the extra pawn with a lead in development.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 f5.name: Modern Defence: Fianchetto Gambit
1.e4 g6 2.d4 f5.strategy: Loses a pawn: 3.exf5 gxf5? walks into 4.Qh5#, so Black has to develop instead, and 4.fxg6 hxg6 leaves Black a pawn down.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn: 3.Bxg5 wins it, because the e7-pawn blocks the queen's diagonal and nothing else defends g5, and the kingside is weakened for nothing.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.e5.strategy: Chases the knight at once and gains space with tempo. The pawn on e5 cramps Black, but it advances early and becomes a target that Black will undermine.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and protects e4 but lets the knight stay on f6: after ...d6 Black has a solid, comfortable game and White's edge is small. White gives up 3.e5, which gains space with tempo.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move, but the bishop blocks the queen's protection of d4, so that pawn stands unguarded. White also gives up 3.e5, which drives the knight off with tempo, and the game is roughly level.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.e5 Nh5.strategy: The knight goes to the rim rather than to d5, where c4 would hit it again. Black loses time, but White's e-pawn is overextended and the knight eyes squares on f4 and g3. A provocative way to lure White forward.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5.strategy: Centralises the knight, but White's c-pawn can chase it again at once, gaining space with a tempo. Black stays sound and keeps the fianchetto plan, but White builds a broad centre and Black has to undermine it later.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.e5 Ng8.strategy: Retreats to the starting square. Nothing is lost on the board, but Black has spent two moves to be back where it began, while White's e5 pawn takes space for free.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4.strategy: Hangs the knight: the queen on d1 takes it at once along the open diagonal and nothing recaptures. The attack on e5 looks tempting but is far too slow.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.e5 Nh5 4.Be2.strategy: Develops with a threat on the rim knight: Bxh5 gxh5 Qxh5 would win a pawn, so Black must retreat or give a pawn for activity. A direct, testing try that wins a useful move, but the bishop stands less well than a quiet defence of e5.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.e5 Nh5 4.g4.strategy: Drives the knight off at once and gains space, but the g-pawn no longer guards f3 and h3, and White has loosened its king's side before developing a piece. The knight simply retreats to g7, and White is the one with the weaknesses.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.e5 Nh5 4.Nf3.strategy: Guards the advanced pawn while developing, so White keeps the space it has gained without committing to anything sharp. The knight on h5 stays offside, and Black needs time to bring it back or to undermine e5.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.e5 Nh5 4.Be2 d6.name: Modern Defence: Norwegian Defence, Norwegian Gambit
1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.e5 Nh5 4.Be2 d6.strategy: Ignores the threat and strikes at the e5 pawn. If White takes the knight, the recapture opens the g-file, and that file with a bishop coming to g7 is Black's compensation for the pawn. A double-edged gambit that demands accurate play from both sides.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.e5 Nh5 4.Be2 Ng7.strategy: Retreats the knight at once and keeps the material. Safe, but the knight stands on the fianchetto bishop's natural square and Black has lost time in the opening, facing a cramping pawn on e5. Sound but passive.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.e5 Nh5 4.Be2 Bg7.strategy: Develops the bishop and hits e5, but the knight is still attacked: White takes it and the queen wins the h5 pawn, and the bishop on g7 blocks the open g-file that is Black's compensation.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nf6 3.e5 Nh5 4.Be2 Ng3.strategy: Looks like a fork of the rook on h1 and the bishop on e2, but it hangs the knight: the h-pawn simply takes it, and Black has nothing to show for the piece.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.c4.strategy: Builds a three-pawn centre while Black's knight stands awkwardly on the rim. Black has no quick way to challenge it, and White can build on the space for a long time.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3.strategy: A natural developing move that supports a later central advance and keeps the c-pawn flexible. White develops while Black's knight is badly placed on the rim.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight and covers d4 and e5 while Black's knight stands on the rim. White does not have to settle the pawns yet and can still trade the dark bishop for the knight whenever it suits. The lead in space and development is the long-term trump.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Bxh6.strategy: Trades the bishop for the awkward knight at once, which cures Black's problem. Black recaptures with the bishop, which then eyes c1, and gets the two bishops. White has given up its own dark bishop and the edge that the misplaced knight offered.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.c4 f6.name: Adams Defence
1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.c4 f6.strategy: Gives the knight the f7 square and holds e5, but the pawn shuts the long diagonal on which the bishop would stand and loosens the a2-g8 diagonal. White's three-pawn centre keeps plenty of time to expand.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.c4 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop looks down the long diagonal at d4, and a knight on h6 does not block it. If White trades on h6, Black recaptures with the bishop and the awkward knight is gone. Otherwise Black waits for White's wide centre to become a target.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.c4 d6.strategy: A solid move: the pawn controls e5, so the e-pawn cannot advance for free, and the c8 bishop is freed. Black accepts White's space and plans to undermine the centre later. The knight on h6 still has no good square and the fianchetto has to follow.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3 f5.strategy: Hits e4 and gives the h6 knight a job, but it is a dubious pawn gambit: White trades the dark bishop for the knight and takes on f5, a clean pawn up with Black's kingside loosened.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop aims along the long diagonal at d4, and a knight on h6 does not get in its way. Black accepts White's wide centre and plans to attack it from a distance, with the awkward knight left to find a better square.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3 d6.strategy: Takes e5 away from White's pawn and frees the c8 bishop. A solid, patient reply, but a slow one: the knight on h6 still lacks a good square and the bishop has yet to reach g7.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3 f5 4.Bxh6.strategy: Trades the bishop for the knight that supports f5. The recapture drags the f8 bishop to h6, off the long diagonal, and White can then take the pawn on f5. The price is the bishop pair.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3 f5 4.exf5.strategy: Takes the pawn at once, but Black regains it with the knight, which lands on f5 and hits d4. Taking back with the g-pawn would lose a pawn to a queen check on h5, so Black has an easy answer. White passes up the clean extra pawn that the bishop trade wins.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3 f5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and covers d4 and e5, but lets Black trade on e4: after ...fxe4 Nxe4 the tension is gone, material is level and the knight on h6 is left in peace. White passes up the extra pawn that the bishop trade wins.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3 f5 4.Bf4.strategy: Develops the bishop with a hit on the knight on h6 and an eye on c7, and keeps the choice of trading on h6 or taking on f5 for later. Black's knight stays offside, and White is ahead in space and development.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3 f5 4.Bxh6 Bxh6.strategy: The only recapture. The bishop does at least get an active diagonal, pointing at d2 and c1, but the plan of a fianchetto on g7 is gone and White can take the pawn on f5.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3 f5 4.Bxh6 fxe4.strategy: Takes a pawn but loses a piece: Bxf8 captures the bishop, and after Black recaptures White also wins back the e4 pawn. Black ends up a knight down.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3 f5 4.Bxh6 Bg7.strategy: Attacks the bishop on h6, but White moves first: Bxg7 takes the bishop with nothing to recapture it, so Black is two pieces down.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3 f5 4.Bxh6 Bxh6 5..strategy: Takes the pawn that Black offered. White is a pawn up, and the pawn on f5 attacks g6, so Black has to find something in return for it.

Develops the knight, but lets Black trade pawns on e4, so material is level and the free pawn is gone. The bishop on h6 still makes the queen's route to d2 and long castling uncomfortable, but White has thrown away its advantage.

Declines the free pawn for a cramping centre. Black keeps the f5 pawn and undermines e5 with ...d6, while the bishop on h6 makes d2 and c1 awkward for White's queen. A fine position, but a pawn less than White could have.

1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3 f5 4.Bxh6 Bxh6 5..name: Modern Defence: Masur Gambit
1.e4 g6 2.d4 Nh6 3.Nc3 f5 4.Bxh6 Bxh6 5..strategy: Castles at once, but the king's side has too few defenders: Bd3 aims at g6, and after fxg6 hxg6 Qg4 White wins a second pawn. Black has to fight in the centre first.

Retreats the bishop to the long diagonal, where it presses on d4, but loses its watch over c1 and d2 and does nothing about the pawn on f5. White keeps the extra pawn and a free development, and Black has spent a tempo on the retreat.
Hits d4 at once and brings a piece into play, so that after fxg6 hxg6 Black has some activity for the lost pawn. The knight blocks the c-pawn, and the pawn is still gone.
Strikes at the centre and opens the c8 bishop onto the pawn on f5, so Black threatens to win it back at once. White can keep the extra pawn with fxg6 hxg6, but Black gets some play for it.
